title: Calculate Salaries
statement:
One table lists every employee's salary before tax:

- `Salaries(company_id, employee_id, employee_name, salary)`: one row per employee of a company; the pair `(company_id, employee_id)` is unique, so the same `employee_id` can appear in several companies.

Each company has a single tax rate, chosen by the **highest** salary paid inside that company:

- 0% when that highest salary is below 1000,
- 24% when it lies between 1000 and 10000, both ends included,
- 49% when it is above 10000.

Report every employee with the columns `company_id`, `employee_id`, `employee_name` and `salary`, where `salary` is the salary after the company's tax is taken off, rounded to the nearest whole number (halves round up). Rows may come in any order.
constraints: The tax rate depends on the company's maximum salary: < 1000 → 0%, 1000..10000 → 24%, > 10000 → 49%
reference:
WITH company_max AS (
  SELECT company_id, employee_id, employee_name, salary,
         MAX(salary) OVER (PARTITION BY company_id) AS max_salary
  FROM Salaries
),
taxed AS (
  SELECT company_id, employee_id, employee_name, salary,
         CASE
           WHEN max_salary < 1000 THEN 0
           WHEN max_salary <= 10000 THEN 24
           ELSE 49
         END AS tax_percent
  FROM company_max
)
SELECT company_id, employee_id, employee_name,
       ROUND(salary * (100 - tax_percent) / 100) AS salary
FROM taxed;
brute:
SELECT s.company_id, s.employee_id, s.employee_name,
       ROUND(s.salary * CASE
         WHEN m.top < 1000 THEN 100
         WHEN m.top > 10000 THEN 51
         ELSE 76
       END / 100) AS salary
FROM Salaries AS s
JOIN (SELECT company_id, MAX(salary) AS top FROM Salaries GROUP BY company_id) AS m
  ON m.company_id = s.company_id
notes:
## Intuition

The tax rate belongs to the company, not to the employee: a clerk earning 300 is taxed at 49% if anyone in the same company earns more than 10000. So every row first needs its company's maximum salary next to it. A window function `MAX(salary) OVER (PARTITION BY company_id)` attaches that maximum to each row without collapsing the rows, which a plain `GROUP BY` would do.

## Approach

1. `company_max`: keep every employee row and add `max_salary`, the largest salary in the same company.
2. `taxed`: turn `max_salary` into a whole-number `tax_percent` of 0, 24 or 49 with a `CASE`, testing the brackets from the lowest up.
3. Final `SELECT`: keep `(100 - tax_percent)` percent of the salary and `ROUND` it to an integer, naming the result `salary` again.

## Example 1, step by step

- Company 1: `max_salary = 21300` (above 10000), so `tax_percent = 49`. Tony keeps 2000 · 51 / 100 = 1020, Pronub 10863, Tyrrox 5508.
- Company 2: `max_salary = 700` (below 1000), so `tax_percent = 0`. Pam, Bassem and Hermione keep 300, 450 and 700.
- Company 3: `max_salary = 7777` (inside 1000..10000), so `tax_percent = 24`. Bocaben keeps 76, Ognjen 1672, Nyancat 2508, and Morninngcat 7777 · 76 / 100 = 5910.52, which rounds to 5911.

## Complexity

- Time: O(n log n) for n rows, to partition the rows by company for the window; the rest is one pass.
- Space: O(n) for the intermediate tables.

## Pitfalls

- Choosing the rate from each employee's own salary instead of the company's maximum taxes low earners in rich companies too lightly.
- The middle bracket includes both 1000 and 10000; writing `< 10000` or `<= 1000` for the neighbours shifts those exact maxima into the wrong rate.
- Truncating instead of rounding (`FLOOR`, integer casts) turns 5910.52 into 5910 and 76.5 into 76.

## Clauses

| Name | Meaning |
| --- | --- |
| `company_max` | every employee row plus `max_salary`, the company's top salary |
| `max_salary` | `MAX(salary)` over the rows sharing `company_id` |
| `taxed` | every employee row with its company's `tax_percent` |
| `tax_percent` | 0, 24 or 49, chosen from `max_salary` |
| `salary` (output) | the salary after tax, rounded to an integer |

narration.1: The first stage keeps every employee and adds the company-wide figure the tax depends on.
narration.3: The window MAX looks at all rows of the same company, so each row learns its company's top salary without being grouped away.
narration.6: The second stage turns that top salary into a tax rate.
narration.9: A company whose highest salary is below 1000 pays no tax.
narration.10: Otherwise a top salary of at most 10000 (1000 and 10000 included) means a 24% rate.
narration.11: Any company paying someone more than 10000 is taxed at 49%.
narration.16: Each employee keeps (100 - tax_percent) percent of the salary, rounded to the nearest integer.
